bib.title: A Comprehensive Survey on Applications of Transformers for Deep Learning Tasks
bib.venue: preprint (cover line: submitted to Expert Systems With Applications, Elsevier, for possible publication)

read.skipped: Reference list (after char ~4591 lines) was only skimmed to its first entries; the lineage uses in-text citations.

question: Which transformer models have been proposed for which deep-learning tasks across NLP, vision, multimodal, audio and speech, and signal processing, and how can they be organised by application?
contributions: A taxonomy of transformer models by five application fields and their tasks (Figure 5).
A count of how many transformer models were proposed per field, 2017 to 2022.
Tables of selected models per task with year, encoder or decoder, pretraining and fine-tuning datasets.
Future directions: wireless networks, cloud computing, medical data, reinforcement learning.

results.claim: The authors collected more than 650 transformer-based models published 2017 onward, about 250 of them for NLP (around 40%).
results.setup: Authors' own literature search of libraries and venues, 2017 to 2022; counts are approximate and the search is not reproducible (no query log or date cut).
results.quote: Our analysis revealed approximately 250 transformer-based models for NLP, representing around 40% of the total

results.claim: Natural image processing accounts for 20% of the collected transformer models and medical image processing 11%, together 31%.
results.quote: combinedly they accounted for 31% of transformer-based models
results.note: Section 3 and Table 1 give 197 relevant papers for computer vision; Section 5 says about 200.

results.claim: About 90 models were multimodal (15%), about 70 audio and speech (11%), and only 4% were signal processing.
results.quote: Finally, only 4% of transformer models were recorded for signal processing.

results.claim: More than 600 models were examined and 99 were selected for the taxonomy (25 NLP, 27 vision, 20 multimodal, 16 audio and speech, 11 signal).
results.setup: Selection criteria are five qualitative ones (first for a task, new attention or position encoding, high citations, real-world application, community buzz).
results.quote: As we have examined more than 600 transformer models during this process
results.note: Section 3 says more than 600; Section 5 says more than 650. The 99 is a sum of the Table 1 column (25+27+20+16+11), not printed by the paper.

results.claim: GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters and works across tasks without gradient updates or fine-tuning.
results.setup: Background description of Brown et al. 2020.
results.quote: in 2020, the largest pre-trained version of GPT with 175 billion parameters, called GPT-3, was released

results.claim: A RoBERTa-large rule-reasoning model reached 98% on the RuleTaker test set, but models trained on it scored 57.7% (T5) and 59.6% (RoBERTa) on harder SAT-derived instances.
results.setup: RuleTaker (Clark et al. 2020b) and the hard-instance dataset of Richardson & Sabharwal 2022; deductive reasoning from natural-language rules.
results.quote: The results showed that the models achieved an accuracy of 57.7% and 59.6% for T5 and RoBERTa, respectively.
results.note: Quoted from other papers; setup details (train size, splits) are not given here.

results.claim: GPT-f, a decoder-only prover, was trained on about 38,000 proofs from set.mm; its largest model has 36 layers and 774M parameters.
results.setup: Polu & Sutskever 2020; automated theorem proving in Metamath.
results.quote: The largest model investigated by the authors consists of 36 layers and 774 million trainable parameters.

results.claim: The survey describes the Switch Transformer as having a permutation-based routing mechanism and a gating mechanism that decides classification versus segmentation; Section 6.1.2 then describes it correctly as replacing the FFN with a switch layer of multiple FFNs.
results.quote: The Switch transformer replaces the feed-forward neural network (FFN) with a switch layer that contains multiple FFNs
results.note: The 6.1.1 description does not match the Switch Transformer paper; treat the survey's model summaries as unreliable.

results.claim: I-GPT variant sizes are printed as IGPT-S 76M, IGPT-M 455M, IGPT-L 1.4B and IGPT-XL 6.8M.
results.note: The 6.8M for XL contradicts the stated pattern that larger variants have more parameters; the source paper's figure is 6.8B. Do not cite this number.

limits: Survey only: no experiments, and no benchmark scores are compared across models; tables list datasets, not results.
Search method is loose (keywords, no dates, no inclusion log), and model counts are approximate; the totals differ between sections (600 vs 650).
Selection of 99 models rests on five qualitative criteria applied by the authors.
Covers 2017 to 2022 only, so the scaling-law, instruction-tuning and open-weight LLM era (Chinchilla, Llama, GPT-4) is absent; InstructGPT is the newest NLP entry.

Several model summaries are wrong or garbled (Switch Transformer routing in 6.1.1, ELECTRA described as masked-LM plus discriminator, CLIP said to generate images, Whisper said to target low-volume speech, DALL-E 2 given 175B parameters, IGPT-XL 6.8M, RoBERTa 'designed for masked language modeling and next sentence prediction'). Do not use its model descriptions as a primary source.
NLP coverage is thin on decoder-only LLMs: GPT family gets one paragraph and Table 4 to 7 repeat the same few models.
practices: Choose a model for a task by looking up its field and task in the taxonomy tables (Section 6, Tables 3 to 27).

Prefer pretrained encoder, decoder or encoder-decoder variants by task: encoder for understanding, decoder for generation, both for translation and summarisation (inferred from the Architecture column of Tables 3 to 9).

the application of deductive reasoning to derive a conclusion from the given premises and rules that are represented in natural language
Single-stream models encode both modalities (text and image) within the same module; two-stream models process text and image through separate modules.
